faqSubtitle: Quick answers on limits, privacy and results.
faq1A: HEIC stands for High Efficiency Image Container. Apple introduced it with iOS 11 as the default photo format for iPhones and iPads. HEIC files are typically 40-50% smaller than equivalent JPGs at similar visual quality — ideal for device storage, but not widely supported outside the Apple ecosystem.
faq2Q: Why can't I open HEIC files on Windows or Android?
faq2A: HEIC is an Apple-proprietary format. Windows requires a paid codec from the Microsoft Store to open HEIC natively, and most Android devices and web platforms don't support it at all. Converting to JPG is the quickest way to make your photos universally accessible.
faq3Q: Will I lose quality converting HEIC to JPG?
faq3A: We convert at 92% JPG quality, which is visually indistinguishable from the original for most uses. The only real trade-off is that JPG uses lossy compression, so you'll see a very slight reduction in quality compared to the lossless HEIC source — but it's imperceptible at normal viewing sizes.
faq4Q: How long are my files kept on the server?
faq4A: Your uploaded HEIC files and converted JPGs are automatically deleted within 1 hour. Once you close the download page, they're gone — we don't keep any copies.
faq5Q: Is this converter free for commercial use?
faq5A: Yes — you can use it for personal or commercial work. No watermarks and no attribution required. The free plan allows 5 uses per day and has a file-size limit; paid plans raise them.
diveSubtitle: The technical details behind why this conversion exists at all.
dive1Title: Why iPhones use HEIC in the first place
dive1Desc: Apple switched to HEIC as the default photo format starting with iOS 11, built on the HEVC video codec. HEVC compresses far more efficiently than JPG's much older codec, storing similar visual quality in 40-50% less space — so your iPhone holds more photos, and iCloud syncs and backups move faster.
dive2Title: HEIC vs. JPG: the real technical difference
dive2Desc: The gap isn't about quality — it's about the codec underneath. HEVC (HEIC) is a modern, efficient video-derived codec; JPEG's compression algorithm dates to 1992. JPG's real advantage isn't technical, it's universal: every device, browser, and app on earth can open it, which HEIC still can't claim.
dive3Title: Where HEIC just works: iPhone, iPad, and Mac
dive3Desc: Photos, Preview, and Quick Look all open HEIC natively with zero conversion. If your photos never leave Apple's ecosystem — iPhone to Mac to iPad — you'll likely never notice the format at all. The friction only appears the moment a HEIC file needs to leave that ecosystem.
dive4Title: Where HEIC breaks: Windows, Android, and the web
dive4Desc: Older Windows builds can't open .heic without installing a codec from the Microsoft Store, most Android phones don't support it out of the box, and a large share of upload forms, editing tools, and websites reject the format outright. Converting to JPG first sidesteps every one of those "unsupported file type" errors.
dive5Title: Does the JPG actually look the same?
dive5Desc: Converting between two lossy formats always re-encodes the image, so there's technically some quality loss. We convert at 92% JPG quality specifically because, at that setting, the difference from the HEIC source is invisible at normal viewing and printing sizes — you're trading an imperceptible amount of quality for universal compatibility.
dive6Title: What happens to your photo's EXIF metadata
dive6Desc: Camera model, date taken, exposure settings, and GPS location (if enabled) are all stored as EXIF metadata inside the file. That metadata carries over into the converted JPG, so photo-organizing apps, cloud backups, and location-based sorting keep working exactly the same after conversion.
seo1Title: HEIC vs JPG — Which Format Should You Use?
seo1P1: Apple switched to HEIC as the default iPhone photo format in 2017 with iOS 11. The main advantage is file size: a HEIC photo is typically 40–50% smaller than the equivalent JPG, which is why an iPhone can fit noticeably more photos in the same storage.
seo1P2: The problem is compatibility. HEIC is an Apple-first format, and while macOS opens it natively, Windows requires extra software, Android doesn't support it, and most web platforms convert or reject it. If you need your photos to work anywhere — in emails, on social media, in design software, or at a print shop — JPG is still the safest choice.
seo2Title: When Do You Need to Convert HEIC to JPG?
seo2P: The most common reason is platform rejection. Instagram, Twitter, and many website upload forms either silently convert your HEIC files (with unpredictable quality) or refuse them entirely. Sending HEIC files via email to non-Apple users, uploading to Google Photos without auto-convert, or opening photos on a Windows PC are all situations where converting to JPG first saves headaches.
